How Urban Trees Cool Cities

By Priya Raman

On the hottest afternoons of the year, the difference between a tree-lined street and a bare one can be felt immediately. Researchers measuring surface and air temperatures across twelve European cities found that neighbourhoods with dense canopy cover were consistently cooler than those with little shade, sometimes by several degrees.

Trees cool their surroundings in two main ways. Their leaves block incoming sunlight before it reaches asphalt and brick, and they release water vapour through their leaves in a process known as evapotranspiration, which draws heat from the air around them.

Unequal shade

The benefits are not shared evenly. The study found that lower-income districts typically had far less canopy than wealthier ones, partly because of historic planning decisions and partly because new developments in those areas left little room for planting. Residents of these districts were therefore more exposed during heatwaves.

City officials interviewed for the study said that planting programmes now prioritise areas with the least shade, but they cautioned that young trees take a decade or more to provide meaningful cooling, so the gap will not close quickly.

What cities are doing

Several cities have set targets to increase canopy cover by a fixed percentage over the next two decades. The researchers argue that these targets should be paired with protection for existing mature trees, which deliver most of the cooling benefit and are often removed during construction.

The authors conclude that urban forests are among the most cost-effective tools for adapting cities to rising temperatures, provided that planting and maintenance budgets are sustained over many years.
